tagline: Hairpins and hydroelectric lakes on the crossing over Washington Pass
intro: The North Cascades Scenic Highway climbs from the Skagit Valley through a narrow canyon, bends past Diablo Lake and crosses Rainy and Washington passes into the Methow Valley. It is a Washington State Scenic Byway and a National Forest Scenic Byway. State of Washington Tourism presents the 140-mile drive as a journey through mountain peaks and glacial lakes, with three hours of driving time.

The first state effort followed a different crossing: work began on a Cascade Pass wagon road in 1897, but floods destroyed most of it. Later, development of the Skagit hydroelectric project encouraged highway promoters to pursue Washington Pass. Politicians, lobbyists and business owners formed the North Cascades Highway Association in 1953; the completed highway opened on September 2, 1972. The highway’s arrival also reshaped Winthrop, which renovated its buildings with Old West false fronts and boardwalk sidewalks to attract the new traffic.

Driving east from Sedro-Woolley, follow the Skagit past Concrete and Rockport to Marblemount, then continue through Newhalem to Diablo Lake. A long hairpin skirts the lake’s southern arm before the road reaches Ross Lake and climbs toward the passes. Beyond Washington Pass, another hairpin begins the descent toward Mazama, followed by Winthrop and Twisp along the Methow River.

moments.title: Concrete
moments.text: Concrete’s name joined two separate cement-making towns on opposite sides of the Baker River. Cement City developed with the Washington Portland Cement Company in 1905; Baker gained a Superior Portland Cement Company plant in 1908. The communities merged as Concrete in 1909. The town sits where the Baker meets the Skagit, and its tall cement silos appear in the film This Boy’s Life. The lower Baker River divides the town, which lies mostly on the Skagit’s north bank. Mount Baker stands to the northwest, with Mount Shuksan almost directly north.
moments.notice: Look for the tall cement silos that appear in This Boy’s Life.

moments.title: Diablo Lake
moments.text: Diablo Lake’s turquoise water carries finely ground rock from surrounding glaciers, suspended as glacial flour. The water itself is held by Diablo Dam, between Ross and Gorge lakes on the Skagit River. Construction finished in 1930, and the dam began operating in 1936 as part of Seattle City Light’s hydroelectric project. The highway curves around the southern arm, crosses a narrow part of the reservoir and passes a scenic viewpoint. Diablo’s company town was established to house the dam builders. When completed, the 389-foot dam was the tallest in the world.
moments.notice: The lake’s turquoise color comes from glacial flour suspended in the water.

moments.title: Washington Pass
moments.text: From the Washington Pass overlook, Liberty Bell Mountain shares the view with the highway 700 feet below. The pass reaches 5,477 feet. The overlook drew an estimated 8,000 visitors during the highway’s first weekend in 1972. Its 0.2-mile trail received National Recreation Trail designation in 1978. A paved trail leads to views of Liberty Bell’s jagged peaks. Winter closes this crossing: snowfall and avalanche risk interrupt through travel each year. The Washington State Department of Transportation explains that closure dates vary by season, keeping the route open as long as possible.
moments.notice: Liberty Bell Mountain and the highway 700 feet below are visible from the overlook.

practical: Washington Pass: The highway closes each winter for snowfall and avalanche risk, typically between mileposts 134 and 171 from late November until late April or early May. (checked 2026-10-11)
